title: Calculate Your Gross Salary: Hourly to Annual with Casual Loading and Super
description: Learn how to convert your hourly rate to annual gross salary using a 38-hour week. Includes casual loading, super paid on top, and tax estimates for 2026–27.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee on the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, the annual gross salary is $52,260.64 based on a 38-hour week; casual employees receive $33.05 per hour including 25% loading, giving an annual gross salary of $65,325.80, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual gross salary from my hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. For example, $26.44 per hour × 38 × 52 = $52,260.64 annual gross salary. This assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. If you are casual, add 25% loading to your base rate before calculating.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the legal minimum for award/agreement-free employees, set at $26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026. Award rates are higher minimums set by the Fair Work Commission for specific industries or occupations, such as the Health Services Award or the SCHADS Award. You must be paid at least the award rate that covers your job. Check the Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides for your award.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my gross salary and super?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. For example, a base rate of $26.44 becomes $33.05 per hour. Your annual gross salary is calculated on the loaded rate. Superannuation (12% of ordinary earnings) is paid on top of your gross salary, not deducted from it. So a casual earning $33.05 per hour receives super calculated on that loaded rate.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Gross Salary

Your **gross salary** is the total amount you earn before any deductions like tax or superannuation. It’s the starting point for budgeting, comparing job offers, and planning your finances. Whether you’re paid by the hour or on a salary, converting between the two helps you see the full picture. This guide explains how to calculate your annual gross salary from an hourly rate, using the standard 38-hour week, and covers casual loading and super paid on top.

### The Formula for Annual Gross Salary

The basic formula is simple: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. For a full-time employee working 38 ordinary hours each week, that’s:

- Annual gross salary = hourly rate × 38 × 52

For example, the [National Minimum Wage](/topics/minimum-wage) from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour. Multiply by 38 hours gives $1,004.90 per week, and by 52 weeks gives $52,260.64 per year. This matches the Fair Work Commission’s published weekly rate of $1,004.90 for a 38-hour week.

If you work fewer or more hours, adjust the weekly hours in the formula. The [timesheet](/) on this site lets you enter your base hourly rate and automatically calculates annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures.

### National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage applies to employees not covered by an award or agreement. However, most Australian workers are covered by an industry or occupation award, which sets higher minimum pay rates. For example, the Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides show that from 1 October 2026, eligible health professionals under the Health Services Award receive increased minimum rates, and from 1 December 2026, home care disability employees under the SCHADS Award get an initial increase of up to 15%. Always check the correct award for your job to ensure you’re paid at least the minimum.

Award rates often include classifications, allowances, and penalty rates that can increase your gross salary beyond the base rate. The formula above gives a baseline; actual earnings may be higher.

### Casual Loading Explained

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (annual leave, sick leave, etc.). This loading is part of your **gross salary** and must be included when calculating annual pay. On the [timesheet](/), you can check a box to add 25% casual loading to your base rate. **Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading** – the calculator adds it for you.

For example, a base rate of $26.44 per hour becomes $33.05 per hour with loading. Annual gross salary then becomes $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,325.80. This is the amount before tax and super.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Superannuation (super) is an additional payment your employer makes into your super fund. It is **paid on top** of your gross salary, not deducted from it. The super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For an employee earning $52,260.64 annual gross salary, the employer contributes an extra $6,271.28 in super (12% of $52,260.64). For a casual on $65,325.80, super is $7,839.10. This extra amount is not part of your take-home pay but builds your retirement savings. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

### Using the Timesheet Calculator

Our [timesheet](/) is designed to make these calculations easy. Enter your base hourly rate, select whether you are casual (to add 25% loading), and the tool shows your:

- Weekly gross salary (based on 38 hours)
- Fortnightly gross salary (weekly × 2)
- Annual gross salary (weekly × 52)
- Estimated superannuation (12% on top)
- Estimated tax using the 2026–27 resident tax scale and Medicare levy

You can also adjust hours if you work a different pattern. The results are estimates – for precise figures, consult your payslip or use the Australian Taxation Office’s gross pay estimator.

### Tax Considerations

Tax is calculated on your gross salary after any pre-tax deductions. For the 2026–27 income year, the resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% of excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 + 30% of excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 + 37% of excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,420 + 45% of excess over $190,000

Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income, with reductions for low-income earners (using 2025–26 thresholds as 2026–27 reductions were not confirmed). For a full-time minimum wage earner ($52,260.64), tax would be approximately $4,020 + 30% of ($52,260.64 – $45,000) = $6,198.19, plus Medicare of $1,045.21, leaving take-home pay around $45,017.24. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool for a detailed estimate.

### Fortnightly and Weekly Breakdown

Knowing your gross salary per pay period helps with budgeting. For a 38-hour week:

- Weekly: hourly rate × 38
- Fortnightly: weekly × 2
- Monthly: annual ÷ 12 (approximately)

For the National Minimum Wage: weekly $1,004.90, fortnightly $2,009.80, monthly $4,355.05. Casual rates: weekly $1,256.13, fortnightly $2,512.26, monthly $5,443.82. These figures are before tax and super.

### Summary

Your **gross salary** is the foundation for understanding your earnings. Use the formula hourly × 38 × 52 for full-time annual pay, add 25% for casual loading, and remember super is paid on top. Always check the relevant award or agreement for your correct minimum rate. For personalised calculations, visit the [timesheet](/) or explore our [pay guides](/blog) for award-specific information.
